category.name: Archives & Historical Web
category.description: Finding what a page used to say and proving what you saw. Web archives are both a research source and the foundation of evidential practice: content that matters gets deleted, and an investigation that did not archive as it went cannot show its work.

tools.name: Wayback Machine
tools.summary: The Internet Archive's web archive — hundreds of billions of captures spanning three decades, free to use and to save into.
tools.description:
The Wayback Machine holds dated snapshots of web pages going back to 1996 and lets anyone both retrieve historical captures and trigger a new capture of a live URL on demand.

Both halves matter. Retrieval answers what a page said before it was edited or removed — a deleted staff page, an amended press release, a company's earlier description of itself. On-demand saving is the single cheapest piece of evidential hygiene available: capturing a page the moment you find it means that when it disappears, you have a third-party-hosted, timestamped record that you did not create and cannot be accused of fabricating.

Its CDX API also exposes the full capture history programmatically, which is how you find the dates a page changed rather than reading snapshots one by one — a fast way to identify exactly when a claim was quietly removed.

Limits: coverage is incomplete and uneven, driven by crawler priorities and by what people asked to save. Site owners can request exclusion, and robots.txt has historically affected availability. JavaScript-heavy pages frequently archive badly or not at all, and an archived page's embedded resources may load from the live web, producing a snapshot that is not what it appears. Absence of a capture proves nothing.
tools.costNotes: Free to search, retrieve and save. Operated by the Internet Archive, a non-profit funded by donations. No account is required for basic use, though an account enables some saving features.
tools.legalNotes: Retrieving and citing archived pages is standard practice in journalism and litigation. Archived material remains subject to its original copyright — an archive copy is not a licence to republish. Note that requesting a save causes the Internet Archive to fetch the live URL, which appears in the target's logs as an Internet Archive request; this is normally unremarkable, but for a very small or closely monitored site the timing can be noticed.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Snapshots are faithful captures made by an independent, long-standing non-profit, which is precisely what gives them evidential weight. The failure modes are coverage and rendering rather than integrity: gaps are common, dynamic pages archive poorly, and a snapshot may pull live resources at view time. Always check that the archived page actually shows the content you are relying on, and cite the specific timestamped capture URL, never the bare domain.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established and foundational service. Direct fetching was not possible from this environment during the review, so this entry is marked high rather than verified; there is no indication of any change in status.

tools.name: archive.today
tools.summary: On-demand page archiving that captures rendered pages faithfully, including many the Wayback Machine handles poorly.
tools.description:
archive.today (also reachable at archive.is, archive.ph and other mirror domains) saves a snapshot of a page on request, producing a rendered capture with a screenshot alongside the extracted content.

It succeeds where the Wayback Machine often fails. Because it captures the rendered page, JavaScript-driven sites, social media posts and single-page applications frequently archive far more faithfully here. It also ignores robots.txt-based exclusion, which means it captures material the Wayback Machine will not — a capability that is genuinely useful and also the reason it is more legally contested.

Use both. Two independent archives of the same page, made at the same time by different operators, is materially stronger evidence than one.

Serious operational caveats. Operator identity and jurisdiction are not publicly established, which is a real weakness if the provenance of your evidence may be challenged. Accessibility is unreliable: the operator has been observed returning bad addresses to resolvers using EDNS, several DNS providers have had trouble resolving it, some have blocked it following legal pressure, and Russian authorities blocked it and several of its domains in March 2026. There is no institutional guarantee of persistence.
tools.costNotes: Free to use and to save, no account. Funding and operation are opaque; there is no service commitment and no assurance of long-term persistence.
tools.legalNotes: The operator is not publicly identified and its jurisdiction is unknown, which matters if you may one day need to authenticate a capture or contact the host. It does not honour robots.txt-based exclusion requests, which is legally contested in some jurisdictions and is why some networks block it. The service has been subject to blocking on legal grounds by DNS providers and by state authorities, including a Russian block in March 2026. For evidence that must withstand challenge, pair it with a Wayback Machine capture from an identifiable institution.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Capture fidelity is excellent, frequently better than the Wayback Machine for modern dynamic pages, and the accompanying screenshot is useful corroboration. Institutional reliability is the weak point: unknown operator, no persistence guarantee, and documented access problems across multiple DNS resolvers and jurisdictions. If it is unreachable, try a different mirror domain or resolver before concluding a capture does not exist.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed operating during this review, along with its documented DNS resolution problems, the November 2025 AdGuard DNS blocking episode and the March 2026 blocking by Russian authorities. Operator identity and jurisdiction remain genuinely unknown and are recorded as such rather than guessed.

tools.name: Internet Archive
tools.summary: The broader non-profit archive beyond the web: television news, books, software, audio, government documents and uploaded collections.
tools.description:
Beyond the Wayback Machine, the Internet Archive holds very large collections of non-web material, and several of them are underused in investigations.

The TV News Archive is the standout: searchable closed-caption transcripts of US television news going back years, with the corresponding clips. Being able to search what was said on broadcast television and retrieve the segment is a capability with no real free equivalent, and it is the way to establish what a public figure actually said on air rather than what was reported. Other collections include digitised books and periodicals, government documents, software and audio, plus material uploaded by researchers and organisations.

Limits: coverage of uploaded collections is arbitrary and depends entirely on who contributed what. Search across the whole archive is uneven. Availability of some material has been affected by litigation over the organisation's book-lending programme, which is a separate matter from the web archive but has affected what is accessible.
tools.costNotes: Free to search and access, with a free account needed for some functions such as borrowing and uploading. Non-profit, donation-funded.
tools.legalNotes: Material carries its original copyright and archive access is not a republication licence — this applies with particular force to broadcast clips and books. The organisation has been the subject of significant copyright litigation regarding lending, which has affected availability of some holdings. Government documents and public-domain material are generally freely reusable.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Institutionally credible with strong provenance for its own collections. The TV News Archive is reliable and well timestamped, though closed-caption transcripts contain recognition errors and should be checked against the audio before quoting. Uploaded community collections vary enormously in provenance and reliability and should be treated as untrusted material until the uploader and source are established.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established non-profit. Not fetched during this review; the availability of specific collections has been affected by litigation and should be checked for the collection you need.

tools.name: Common Crawl
tools.summary: Petabyte-scale open corpus of monthly web crawls — raw page content, extracted text and link graphs, free to download.
tools.description:
Common Crawl publishes the raw output of large-scale web crawls: full page responses in WARC format, extracted plain text, metadata, and a link graph, released roughly monthly and hosted for free public download.

This is not a lookup tool. It is a dataset for questions no interactive service will answer — finding every page across the web that contained a particular tracking identifier, mapping which sites linked to a network of domains, or reconstructing text that has since vanished. That kind of question is how coordinated networks of sites get exposed, and Common Crawl is often the only free way to ask it.

It requires real engineering: the archives are enormous, and querying them means either the columnar index with a data-processing framework or substantial cloud compute. Budget for that before planning around it.

Limits: the crawl is broad but not complete, sampling is not uniform, and each crawl is a point-in-time slice rather than continuous coverage. A page's absence from a crawl says nothing about whether it existed.
tools.costNotes: The data is free and openly licensed, published by a non-profit. Your costs are compute and egress: processing meaningful subsets generally means cloud infrastructure, and that bill is real. There is a free hosted index for URL lookups that avoids this for simple queries.
tools.legalNotes: Published as an open dataset for research and analysis, with terms of use to read before redistribution. The corpus contains whatever was on the crawled pages, including personal data — deriving a dataset about individuals from it makes you a controller with full obligations, and 'it was in Common Crawl' is not a lawful basis. The crawler respects robots.txt, which is why some sites are absent.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Faithful captures with documented crawl methodology and dates, which is exactly what reproducible research needs. Coverage is the limitation: broad but not exhaustive, non-uniformly sampled, and shaped by robots.txt exclusions. Conclusions from Common Crawl should always be framed as what appears in a specific dated crawl, never as what exists on the web.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established non-profit dataset with a regular publication cadence. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: Memento Time Travel
tools.summary: Federated lookup that queries many web archives at once for captures of a URL near a given date.
tools.description:
Memento is a protocol for datetime negotiation with web archives, and Time Travel is the aggregator built on it. Give it a URL and a target date and it queries participating archives — the Internet Archive, national libraries, university archives and others — returning captures from any of them near that date.

The reason to use it is that the Wayback Machine is not the only archive, and for non-English and non-US content it is frequently not the best one. A page missing from the Wayback Machine may be well captured by a national library archive that nobody thinks to check. One federated query is far more efficient than visiting each archive by hand.

Caveats are real. It is a research-project service rather than a production one, and its availability and the set of participating archives have varied over time. It is served over plain HTTP at the address given, which is itself a signal about how actively it is maintained. Confirm it is responding before building a workflow around it, and know which archives to query directly as a fallback.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account. Operated as an academic research service without a service commitment.
tools.legalNotes: An aggregator that points to captures held by other archives; each archive's own terms apply to the material you retrieve. Nothing here changes the copyright position of the archived content.
tools.reliabilityNotes: When it works it is genuinely valuable and finds captures other approaches miss. Its reliability is limited by being a research service: uptime is not guaranteed, participating-archive coverage changes, and some member archives respond slowly or not at all, producing incomplete results that look like negatives. Do not treat a null result from Time Travel as evidence no archive holds the page.
tools.confidenceNotes: The Memento protocol and this aggregator are real and well documented in the web-archiving literature, but the service's current operational status, uptime and the present set of participating archives were not verified during this review. It is served over plain HTTP and has a history of intermittent availability. Confirm it responds before relying on it; if it does not, query national and institutional archives directly.

tools.name: UK Web Archive
tools.summary: Legal-deposit archive of the UK web, with far deeper coverage of UK sites than general crawlers.
tools.description:
The UK Web Archive, run by the British Library with the other UK legal deposit libraries, archives the UK web domain under non-print legal deposit legislation. It crawls UK sites comprehensively and annually, alongside curated thematic collections built around events, elections and topics.

For any investigation touching a UK organisation this is worth checking specifically, because its coverage of UK sites is deeper and more systematic than a general-purpose crawler's. Small organisational and political sites that the Wayback Machine sampled thinly are often captured properly here, and the curated collections are professionally assembled around exactly the events researchers care about.

The major constraint is access. Legal deposit terms mean a large portion of the archive is available only on-site in the reading rooms of the deposit libraries, not over the open internet. What is openly available is a subset for which permission was obtained. Plan for a library visit if the material you need is restricted, and note that reading-room access is itself a disclosure of interest in some contexts.
tools.costNotes: Free. Openly available material can be accessed online; a substantial portion is accessible only in the reading rooms of the UK legal deposit libraries under the terms of the legal deposit regulations.
tools.legalNotes: Collected under UK non-print legal deposit legislation, which both authorises the collection and constrains access — the reading-room-only restriction on much of the archive is a statutory condition, not a policy choice. Archived material remains under its original copyright and legal deposit access does not confer republication rights.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Institutional archive with professional curation, documented crawl policies and legal-deposit provenance, which makes captures unusually defensible as evidence. Scope is limited to the UK web domain as defined by the regulations. The main practical limitation is access rather than quality.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established institutional archive backed by statute. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: Library of Congress Web Archives
tools.summary: Curated thematic web archive collections built by US national library subject specialists.
tools.description:
The Library of Congress archives the web selectively rather than comprehensively, building curated collections around themes: elections, legislation, public policy, international events, and the web presence of organisations and movements it judges to be of enduring research value.

Curation is the point and the difference. A subject specialist decided a set of sites mattered and captured them systematically over time, including sites that broad crawlers sampled poorly or missed. For politically sensitive material — campaign sites, advocacy organisations, government pages later altered or removed — a Library of Congress capture also carries institutional weight that a general crawl does not, which matters when your evidence may be challenged.

Limits: coverage is narrow by design and follows the Library's collecting priorities, which are US-centred. If your subject was not in a collection's scope it was not captured, and some archived material carries access restrictions negotiated with site owners.
tools.costNotes: Free to access online, no account required for openly available material. Some captures carry access restrictions agreed with the original site owners.
tools.legalNotes: US national library collection with documented collecting policies. Archived content retains its original copyright and some items have negotiated access restrictions. Citing a Library of Congress capture is straightforward and its provenance is strong.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Professionally curated with documented scope and clear provenance, which makes captures highly defensible. Coverage is deliberately selective and US-focused, so absence indicates only that a subject fell outside a collecting policy. Check the scope note of the relevant collection before drawing any inference from a gap.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established national institution. Not fetched during this review; the Library reorganises its web presence periodically, so confirm the current entry point.
